summary: Defines Multipath TCP, an experimental extension that lets one TCP connection use several network paths and addresses at the same time. This can improve throughput and resilience, while still looking like ordinary TCP to applications. It was replaced by RFC 8684.

eli5.summary: Instead of sending a long line of friends down one hallway, you split them across several hallways. If one hallway is blocked, the rest still get through.

questions: how can tcp use wifi and cellular at once
subtitle: Enables a single TCP connection to simultaneously use multiple network paths and addresses

tldr.problem: Standard TCP connections use a single network path, limiting throughput and resilience even when multiple paths are available between hosts.
tldr.mechanism: Multipath TCP adds extensions to TCP allowing a single connection to operate across multiple paths simultaneously, with data sequence mapping to reassemble segments arriving over different subflows with varying delays, and coupled congestion control to fairly share bandwidth.
tldr.outcome: MPTCP improves resource utilization and resilience, remaining transparent to applications while enabling throughput gains and recovery from partial path failures. It was later updated and superseded by RFC 8684.

today: RFC 6824 is an Experimental protocol that has been superseded by RFC 8684. MPTCP remains an active area of research and implementation, with significant deployments in real-world networks. The protocol has proven feasible despite the challenges of middlebox compatibility, and continues to be refined based on operational experience.

sections.title: Introduction to Multipath TCP
sections.content:
Multipath TCP (MPTCP) is a set of extensions to regular TCP that allows a single TCP connection to operate across multiple network paths simultaneously. This enables hosts to use different paths defined by different source/destination address pairs to exchange data, improving resource utilization and resilience without requiring changes to applications.

MPTCP is designed with three key constraints. First, it must be backwards-compatible with standard TCP to maximize deployment chances. Second, it can assume that one or both hosts are multihomed (have multiple addresses). Third, the protocol must function through existing middleboxes like NATs, firewalls, and proxies, where TCP options might be removed or duplicated. To applications, MPTCP appears as a standard TCP connection providing reliable, ordered bytestream delivery, while the protocol transparently manages multiple underlying TCP flows called subflows.
sections.eli5: MPTCP lets one TCP connection use several paths at the same time, so more data can flow. Applications don't see the difference—it still looks like regular TCP to them, just faster.

sections.title: MPTCP Concepts and Architecture
sections.content:
MPTCP introduces several key terms and concepts. A path is defined by a 4-tuple of source/destination addresses and ports. A subflow is a TCP flow operating over an individual path, and multiple subflows together form one MPTCP connection. Each host is given a unique 64-bit key during connection setup that is hashed to create a token used to identify the connection on subsequent subflows. The data sequence number (DSN) is a 64-bit number applied at the connection level, while each subflow has its own 32-bit sequence number space.

MPTCP operates at the transport layer and aims to be transparent to both applications and the underlying IP layer. The protocol stack shows MPTCP sitting above one or more TCP subflows, which each run over IP. This layering ensures compatibility with existing network infrastructure while providing the multipath capability at a level accessible to applications.
sections.eli5: MPTCP creates multiple regular TCP flows (subflows) between different address pairs, bundles them together, and reassembles the data so the application sees one orderly stream. A key identifies the connection, and a special sequence number tracks data across all the paths.

sections.title: Connection Setup and Subflow Management
sections.content:
MPTCP connection initiation resembles standard TCP but includes the MP_CAPABLE option on SYN, SYN/ACK, and ACK packets. This option allows each host to declare its 64-bit key and verify that the other host supports MPTCP. The keys exchanged are used for authenticating additional subflows through HMAC computation.

Additional subflows are established similarly to regular TCP connections but include the MP_JOIN option containing a token (derived from the initial connection's keys) to identify which MPTCP connection the new subflow joins. The token is essential because it allows demultiplexing of incoming SYN packets to the correct connection without relying on the destination port. When a new subflow is established, both hosts perform an HMAC-based authentication handshake using the keys and random numbers (nonces) exchanged in the MP_JOIN options. This ensures that the new subflow is joining the intended connection and guards against hijacking.

Through this mechanism, subflows can be created between any pair of addresses at the two hosts. The number of subflows can fluctuate during the connection's lifetime, and subflows can fail independently while the overall connection continues.
sections.eli5: When starting an MPTCP connection, both ends swap keys. When adding a new path (subflow), each side proves it knows the keys using a code (HMAC) to prevent hijacking. If one path breaks, the others keep working.

sections.title: Data Transfer and Reassembly
sections.content:
The core challenge in MPTCP is that subflows may have different delays and loss characteristics, so data arriving on different subflows can be out of order. MPTCP solves this with the Data Sequence Signal (DSS) option, which carries two key pieces of information: a data sequence mapping and a data-level acknowledgment (Data ACK).

The data sequence mapping specifies how subflow-level sequence numbers map to the connection-level data sequence space. It consists of starting sequence numbers for both spaces and the length of bytes for which the mapping is valid. This allows a receiver to reassemble segments from multiple subflows into the correct order for delivery to the application, even when they arrive out of order on different subflows.

Subflow-level acknowledgments (regular TCP ACKs) are independent from connection-level acknowledgments. While TCP ACKs on each subflow acknowledge reception on that subflow alone, the Data ACK in the DSS option is a cumulative acknowledgment for data at the connection level. All subflows share the same receive buffer and advertise the same receive window. This allows any subflow to send data as long as the receiver is willing to accept it at the connection level.

The DSS option also includes an optional checksum over the mapped data, used to detect if middleboxes have altered the payload. If a checksum fails, MPTCP can either terminate the broken subflow or fall back to standard TCP for the entire connection.
sections.eli5: Each packet on a subflow carries information saying "this piece of data belongs at position X in the overall stream." The receiver reassembles these pieces in order. Each subflow also sends separate acknowledgments, but the main connection also sends its own ACK tracking progress.

sections.title: Address Management and Path Control
sections.content:
MPTCP supports two complementary methods for establishing additional subflows. Direct subflow setup occurs when a host with an additional address initiates a new subflow by sending a SYN with MP_JOIN to one of the peer's addresses. This is simple and implicit.

The second method uses the ADD_ADDR option to explicitly announce additional addresses on the host. The receiving host can then use this information to initiate new subflows. This mechanism is more robust because it works even when one host is behind a NAT and cannot accept incoming connections. Each advertised address receives an Address ID, which serves as a reference identifier independent of actual IP addresses (allowing operation through address-translating middleboxes).

Corresponding to ADD_ADDR is the REMOVE_ADDR option, used to announce that an address is no longer available. A host receiving this option first verifies the path is truly unavailable before terminating associated subflows. Subflow priority can be controlled using the MP_PRIO option, allowing a host to designate subflows as backup paths (to be used only when primary paths fail) or to change priority during operation.
sections.eli5: A host can start a new subflow from one of its addresses, or tell the other end "I'm also reachable at this address" using ADD_ADDR. The other end can then use that address. If an address goes away, REMOVE_ADDR says so. MP_PRIO can mark paths as backup.

sections.title: Status and Evolution
sections.content:
RFC 6824 is an Experimental protocol published in January 2013. It represents the detailed protocol specification for Multipath TCP, developed alongside complementary documents covering MPTCP architecture, congestion control algorithms, and application considerations. The protocol was designed to be implementable and deployable in the current Internet while providing significant benefits.

The document is superseded by RFC 8684, a more recent version that incorporates experience gained from implementations and deployments of the MPTCP protocol. While experimental, RFC 6824 has been the foundation for multiple open-source and commercial MPTCP implementations and has demonstrated the protocol's feasibility in real-world networks. The protocol continues to evolve as researchers and practitioners identify optimizations and refinements.
sections.eli5: This RFC from 2013 described how to build MPTCP. It was experimental—not yet a standard—but it worked well enough that many people built it. A newer version came out later with improvements based on real-world experience.
